headline: Stocks are expensive, and the AI buildout is absorbing much more cash.

rubric.question: How expensive are stocks relative to earnings?
rubric.readout: Broad-market valuation is historically elevated; this is a valuation warning, not a crash clock.

rubric.question: Can the builders fund the spending?
rubric.readout: The five-company total still generates more operating cash than cash capex, but that cushion is shrinking; Amazon and Oracle individually spend more than OCF.

rubric.question: Is spending translating into growth?
rubric.readout: Revenue and OCF are growing, but capex is growing faster. Company-wide growth does not establish AI project returns.

cape.label: Broad US stocks: price / ten-year average real earnings
cape.definition: Shiller CAPE; broad US market context, not an AI-only or Nasdaq P/E.

sample.percentileDefinition: Percentage of nonmissing complete-month observations at or below current value, including current month

limitations: Reconstructed/revised workbook vintage, not publication-date backtest.
CAPE differs from ordinary trailing P/E. Source earnings are interpolated.
July–August 2026 trailing P/E unavailable because source earnings stop June; do not infer it from CAPE.
Company-wide cash capex and operating cash flow; not AI-specific.
Cash capex excludes noncash finance leases; cash-flow measures do not prove AI return on investment.
Latest current periods: four companies TTM to June 2026; Oracle FY to May 2026. Prior periods are corresponding year-earlier periods.
Historical snapshot date is not the fiscal period end. Actual endpoints retained. Revised companyfacts are not an archived point-in-time backtest.
Dollar-weighted sum(capex)/sum(OCF), not average of company percentages.

historicalCases.name: US railroads · 1873
historicalCases.parallel: Large infrastructure commitments depend on future demand and financing.
historicalCases.difference: No acquired railroad earnings or investment accounts; current buyers have measured operating cash flows.

historicalCases.name: US stocks, 1929
historicalCases.parallel: Same broad-US CAPE denominator permits a meaningful valuation comparison.
historicalCases.difference: This broad-market context does not establish AI-only valuation or 1930s-style bank vulnerability.

historicalCases.name: Gold, 1980
historicalCases.missingReason: Asset itself produces no corporate earnings or sales; miners/producers are separate entities.
historicalCases.parallel: Speculative demand can move asset prices.
historicalCases.difference: Gold itself has no earnings or operating cash flow; corporate P/E and capex/OCF are not applicable.

historicalCases.name: Japan equities, 1989
historicalCases.parallel: High prices relative to earnings can coexist with successful established firms.
historicalCases.difference: Index composition and accounting differ; NRI350 reported P/E is not Shiller CAPE or Nikkei225 P/E.

historicalCases.name: Dot-com, 2000
historicalCases.valuationLabel: US broad market context; not Nasdaq P/E
historicalCases.parallel: Technology optimism and high broad-market CAPE recur.
historicalCases.difference: Two surviving dotcom firms are not the failed startup/telecom population; today’s spending is supported by large company-wide OCF.

historicalCases.name: US housing, 2006
historicalCases.valuationLabel: US house-price/rent index, Dallas Fed 2025 vintage
historicalCases.missingReason: Historical price/rent series acquired; net rental yields and matched leverage remain unavailable.
historicalCases.parallel: Long-lived investment can be exposed to demand disappointment.
historicalCases.difference: Housing uses rental-service prices as a denominator, not corporate earnings. See the separate quarterly housing chart; these indexes do not measure net cash returns.

historicalCases.name: China equities, 2007
historicalCases.difference: Year-end Shanghai P/E is not October peak P/E or matched to the OECD price portfolio.

historicalCases.name: China equities, 2015
historicalCases.parallel: Investor leverage can transmit forced selling.
historicalCases.difference: December P/E is after the June peak; using it as peak valuation would mislead.

historicalCases.name: Bitcoin, 2017
historicalCases.missingReason: Asset itself produces no corporate earnings or sales; miners/producers are separate entities.
historicalCases.parallel: Prices can depend on speculative demand.
historicalCases.difference: Bitcoin itself has no corporate earnings; an AI company earnings comparison is inapplicable.

historicalCases.name: Bitcoin, 2021
historicalCases.missingReason: Asset itself produces no corporate earnings or sales; miners/producers are separate entities.
historicalCases.parallel: Investor losses can be amplified by intermediaries.
historicalCases.difference: Bitcoin earnings/cash-flow ratios are inapplicable; platform failures are distinct from the asset price decline.

classificationNote: Ten main historical cases include US railroads 1873. UK railway mania 1845 is a separate supplemental case: its dividend yields/paid-up capital cannot be used for US railroads. NA is not zero and high valuation is not a calibrated bubble probability.
